architecture_decisions.recommendation: Implemented a three-layer caching hierarchy: LRU cache → Vercel edge cache → Redis → MySQL fallback
architecture_decisions.rationale: This provides graceful degradation during traffic spikes. LRU cache offers fastest in-memory access for hot data. Vercel edge cache (5s TTL) provides short-lived shared cache across serverless instances during scaling events. Redis serves as persistent cache (24h TTL) for consistent data. MySQL is the ultimate source of truth.
alternatives_considered: Single Redis instance for all operations
Using only LRU cache with longer TTL

architecture_decisions.recommendation: Separated Redis instances for different workloads: main Redis for general operations, us-east-1 Redis for high-volume click tracking
architecture_decisions.rationale: Isolates high-volume click tracking operations to prevent them from impacting other Redis-dependent endpoints. If the us-east-1 Redis instance fails, only click tracking is affected, not the entire application. This follows the bulkhead pattern for fault isolation.
alternatives_considered: Single Redis instance with separate databases
Implementing circuit breakers on single Redis instance

architecture_decisions.recommendation: Updated track endpoints to use Promise.all for parallel cache lookups and separated Redis instance usage
architecture_decisions.rationale: Parallelizing cache lookups reduces latency by fetching click IDs and link data concurrently. Separating click ID cache (us-east-1 Redis) from link cache (main Redis) prevents resource contention and allows independent scaling of high-volume operations.
alternatives_considered: Combining all cache operations in single mget
Using Redis pipelines instead of Promise.all

architecture_decisions.recommendation: Enhanced logging throughout the cache hierarchy to track hits/misses at each layer
architecture_decisions.rationale: Provides visibility into cache performance and helps identify bottlenecks. Each cache layer logs its status, making it easier to debug cache behavior during traffic spikes and optimize TTLs based on real usage patterns.

architecture_decisions.recommendation: Updated middleware to use Node.js runtime instead of edge runtime and upgraded @vercel/functions dependency
architecture_decisions.rationale: Node.js runtime provides more stable execution environment for middleware operations. Upgrading to @vercel/functions 3.4.3 enables access to getCache() API for edge caching and ensures compatibility with newer Vercel features.
alternatives_considered: Keeping edge runtime with different caching strategy
Implementing custom cache layer without Vercel functions

architecture_decisions.recommendation: Added try-catch around Vercel cache operations to gracefully handle failures
architecture_decisions.rationale: Ensures that Vercel cache failures don't break the entire caching flow. If Vercel cache is unavailable, the system falls back to Redis and MySQL, maintaining core functionality during infrastructure issues.
alternatives_considered: Using circuit breakers for cache layers

implementation_summary:
The implementation introduces a sophisticated multi-layer caching system designed to protect the Dub application from traffic spikes while maintaining high performance for link lookups and click tracking. The core innovation is a three-tier caching hierarchy: in-memory LRU cache (3s TTL) for fastest access, Vercel edge cache (5s TTL) as a shared fallback during serverless instance scaling, and Redis (24h TTL) as persistent storage. This design ensures that during traffic surges when new Vercel Fluid instances spin up, they can quickly access cached data from the shared Vercel cache rather than hitting Redis or MySQL immediately.

A key architectural decision was separating Redis workloads: click tracking operations (high volume, time-sensitive) were moved to a dedicated us-east-1 Redis instance, while general link data remains in the main Redis instance. This isolation prevents high-volume click operations from impacting other Redis-dependent endpoints, implementing a bulkhead pattern for fault tolerance. The track endpoints were optimized to use Promise.all for parallel cache lookups, reducing latency by fetching click IDs and link data concurrently.

The system integrates gracefully with the existing codebase by extending the existing cache abstraction in lib/api/links/cache.ts and updating the track endpoints to use the new Redis instance separation. Enhanced logging provides observability into cache performance at each layer, helping operators understand cache behavior during traffic spikes. The middleware runtime was changed from edge to Node.js for stability, and the @vercel/functions dependency was upgraded to access the getCache() API needed for the edge caching layer.

This approach balances performance, reliability, and maintainability. During normal operations, most requests hit the LRU cache. During traffic spikes, the Vercel edge cache prevents thundering herd problems on Redis. If any cache layer fails, the system gracefully degrades to the next layer, ensuring core functionality remains available. The separation of Redis instances provides operational resilience, allowing high-volume click tracking to be scaled independently from other Redis operations.
